children.text: Rice terraces carved into the mountainside with stone and earth by the Ifugao people without machinery, a symbol of the Philippines once depicted on the old 20-peso bill. Banaue serves as the gateway to the sweeping view from its viewpoint and to the surrounding World Heritage villages.
Banaue is a village set in a mountain valley about

above sea level, in the middle of Ifugao province in northern Luzon. The mountainsides surrounding the village are carved into hundreds of tiers of paddies from bottom to top, and Filipinos have long proudly called this the "Eighth Wonder of the World." The scene printed on the back of the old Philippine 20-peso bill is exactly this Banaue rice terrace.

The Ifugao people who built the rice terraces stacked stone and mud into paddy walls and created an elaborate irrigation system, splitting water flowing down from the mountaintop forests into bamboo channels that pass water down tier by tier. They are often introduced as "2,000-year-old paddies," but recent archaeological research has also suggested that large-scale terracing may have taken hold in earnest only around 300–400 years ago, roughly around the time of Spanish arrival. Either way, it remains an immense cultural landscape built up over generations through the community's labor and traditional knowledge.
One thing worth knowing is that the "Rice Terraces of the Philippine Cordilleras," inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in

, comprise five areas — Batad, Bangaan, Hungduan (Hapao), Mayoyao, and Nagacadan — and the paddies around Banaue's viewpoint are not included among them. Instead, Banaue serves as the transport hub to these World Heritage villages, and as a base camp gathering accommodation, restaurants, and the tourist information center.
The Banaue Rice Terraces were designated a Philippine National Cultural Treasure in

by Presidential Decree No. 260. They were left off the World Heritage list because many modern buildings had gone up close to the village, so the site fell short of UNESCO's integrity criteria. This scenery appears not only on the old 20-peso bill but also on the back of the old 1,000-peso bill used from

. The Hudhud, an Ifugao epic chant passed down along with rice farming and sung mainly by older women at planting, harvest, and funerals, was inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in

Rather than just taking photos at the viewpoint and leaving, it's recommended to stay a day or two and also do the Batad or Hapao trek, visit traditional house villages, and browse Ifugao woodcarving. It suits travelers who want both culture and scenery, and those combining the trip with Sagada for a Cordillera loop.

3–4km
north of the village center, where you can see the exact scene from the old banknote. You can take photos with Ifugao elders in traditional dress, and it's customary to give a small tip (about

A World Heritage area about
1 hour
by car from Banaue, where you can walk among the terraces spread across a wide valley. The hot spring by the nearby Hapao River is also worth a visit.
A route covering the amphitheater-shaped World Heritage rice terraces and a trip out to Tappiya Falls. It's possible as a day trip from Banaue, but staying overnight is recommended if you can.
A World Heritage village along the way to Batad, where you can look down from a roadside viewpoint at traditional thatched houses clustered in the middle of the rice terraces.

blocks.title: Walking the traditional house villages (Tam-an and Poitan)

children.text: Within walking distance of Banaue's center are villages where traditional Ifugao raised houses remain. Guides explain everyday wisdom built into the structures, such as disc-shaped rat guards fitted onto the posts to keep rodents from climbing up.
Banaue is known for carvings of "bulul," the guardian spirit of the harvest. You can watch artisans carving them in person at village workshops and souvenir shops.
A traditional Ifugao rice wine, essential at rituals and feasts. It's sweet but fairly strong, so sip it a little at a time.

A small private museum next to the Banaue View Inn on the main street, holding Ifugao baskets, weapons, beaded jewelry, clothing, and everyday tools associated with H. Otley Beyer, known as the father of Philippine anthropology. Admission is about
, hours are usually
, and photography is not allowed inside. It is a good place to visit on a rainy day.

On arrival in Banaue, register at the tourist information center on the main street where the buses stop (in the Triage area) and pay the

environmental fee. Banaue Viewpoint is on a hill along the road toward Bontoc, and several more overlooks line the roadside, showing the valley from different angles, so agree with your tricycle driver in advance on where to stop.

To reach Batad you have to walk down from the Saddle Point, where vehicles can go (or the end of the road just below it), and pay a separate
environmental and heritage management fee at the ticket booth on the path into the village. The route from the village to Tappiya Falls goes up and down paddy walls and stone steps and takes
30 minutes–1 hour 30 minutes
one way depending on your pace. The climb back up to the Saddle is continuous, so set out well before dark. For details, see
Batad Rice Terraces
Trek the Hapao rice terraces and visit the hot spring
Lunch, then travel on toward Sagada or Manila
Hapao is about
45 minutes–1 hour
from Banaue by jeepney or tricycle. You register and pay a fee at the entrance, then follow the paddy-wall path on foot to Bogiyah Hot Spring, which takes around
40 minutes–1 hour
. For fares and directions, see
Hungduan and Hapao Rice Terraces

Direct overnight buses run daily from Manila to Banaue. The main operators are Ohayami Trans (terminal at the corner of Lacson Avenue and Fajardo Street, Sampaloc, Manila) and Coda Lines (terminal at the corner of Monte de Piedad Street and Maryland Street, Cubao). The trip takes about
8–10 hours
and the fare is about
. Depending on the company and bus class, buses depart between
and arrive early in the morning.
With Ohayami you can buy seats in advance on the
official booking site
with GCash or a card, and with Coda Lines you buy at the Cubao terminal counter or through an online booking agent. During Holy Week and the year-end holidays they often sell out
1–2 weeks
ahead.
Coda Lines has 45-seat buses and 35-seat buses with a toilet on board, and the 35-seat buses cost slightly more. Buses back from Banaue to Manila usually depart between
There are also buses to Banaue from Baguio, taking about
8–9 hours
via Nueva Vizcaya.
The Ohayami bus from Baguio leaves at night from the terminal on Governor Pack Road and reaches Banaue at dawn. To travel in the daytime, you can go in via Halsema Highway through Sagada and Bontoc.
From Sagada, it's about
1 hour
to Bontoc by jeepney, and about
2–3 hours
from Bontoc to Banaue by van or jeepney.
Head north on NLEX, pass through Nueva Ecija (Cabanatuan and San Jose), cross Dalton Pass, and from Bagabag in Nueva Vizcaya climb up to Banaue via Lamut and Lagawe in Ifugao. It takes about
8–9 hours
, and because the mountain road beyond Lagawe has many bends, daytime driving is recommended.
From Baguio, either take Halsema Highway to Bontoc and come down along the Bontoc–Banaue road, or go past Ambuklao and Kayapa, exit at Aritao in Nueva Vizcaya, and enter via Bagabag and Lagawe.
The nearest international airport is Clark International Airport (CRK), about
7–8 hours
by car. Coming from Tuguegarao Airport (TUG) is also possible, but public transport connections are inconvenient.
To save time, you can fly from Manila to Cauayan Airport (CYZ) in Isabela on Cebu Pacific or PAL Express for about
1 hour
, then drive about
3–4 hours
in a chartered vehicle to Banaue. Transferring by public transport takes more than
5 hours
Within the village, tricycles are the basic mode of transport. A round trip charter to the viewpoint costs about
, and a charter to Batad Saddle Point costs about
(including waiting time).
Shared jeepneys to Batad often depart in the afternoon, so chartering is the more practical option for a day trip.
Shared jeepneys to Hapao and Hungduan mostly run a few times a day after
and take about
1 hour
. If the timing doesn't work, it's better to charter a tricycle or jeepney.
The rice terraces change color with the seasons. Around Banaue, planting is usually done in
January–February
, the paddies fill with green in
March–May
, and the rice ripens to gold and is harvested in
June–July
. After harvest,
August–December
is the period of clearing the fields and flooding them again, when the terrace outlines stand out sharply, giving photos a different kind of appeal. For the paddy scenery alone, the deep green of
April–May
and the golden hue of
June
are the most popular.
For weather, the
December–April
dry season is easier for getting around, but dawns in
December–February
are chilly at around
. In the
June–October
rainy season, rain and fog are frequent, and typhoons can cause landslides on the Lagawe–Banaue road. Banaue's cultural festival "Imbayah" is usually held in
late April–early May
, but whether it takes place and its dates vary each year, so check the tourist information office's announcements to see if your travel timing fits.
Banaue's town center is about
above sea level, so it stays cool all year. In January the average is around
by day and

January–March
and falls almost daily in
May–September

. Imbayah is a festival named after the rice wine bayah, which grew out of the feast ritual that wealthy Kadangyan hosted to raise their social standing, and it features a parade in traditional costume, dancing, a woodcarving contest, wooden scooter races, and folk wrestling. In
it was not held because of the energy crisis. Gotad ad Ifugao, the festival marking the founding of Ifugao province, is held every year for a little over a week up to
June 18
in the provincial capital Lagawe (about
25km
from Banaue).

Accommodation clusters in Banaue's town center (Poblacion), where the buses stop. Many guesthouses overlook the rice terraces and cost about
per night, while places with a pool and spacious rooms, like the long-running government-operated Banaue Hotel, run about

. Banaue is cold at night and doesn't need air conditioning, but be sure to check whether hot showers are available. For a deeper trekking experience, spending a night at a guesthouse inside Batad village is also a good idea.

The food here is simple. Filipino home-style cooking, Ifugao-style smoked pork, and sauteed wild vegetables sold at guesthouse restaurants are the basics, and some places let you taste native rice grown in the terraces, including "tinawon," a reddish traditional variety. Traditional tapuy rice wine, and a morning of hot coffee with pandesal, pair well with the crisp mountain village air.
Tinawon, which means "once a year" in Ifugao, is a native rice that takes
8–10 months

from field preparation to harvest and is therefore harvested only once a year. It is grown without machinery, water buffalo, or chemical fertilizer. Common souvenirs at the viewpoint and in the shops of the town center are bulul wood carvings, knives with carved sheaths, baskets, and Ifugao textiles, and the public market in the town center sells vegetables and daily necessities.
There are a few ATMs in Banaue, but they often break down or run out of cash. Withdraw enough cash in Baguio or Manila beforehand.
The air conditioning on overnight buses is very strong. Bring long sleeves, a blanket, and a neck pillow.
Booking a trekking guide through the tourist information center connects you with an accredited guide at a fixed rate.
Visiting the viewpoint early in the morning lets you see the fog clear and sunlight fall across the paddies, with fewer group tourists around.
Shoes with good grip are essential when walking the paddy walls, and bring spare socks during the rainy season.
It's safer to book your return bus as soon as you arrive.
Mobile data works in the town center but is often cut off in the valley villages. Download offline maps in advance.

Ohayami online bookings can be canceled only up to the day before departure, with a 50% fee. On the day of departure there is no refund, only rebooking. The rules may change, so check them on the booking screen.

Neighboring villages such as Batad and Hapao charge a registration or environmental fee separately at the entrance. This is separate from the environmental fee you paid in Banaue, so bring plenty of small change.
June 18
is Ifugao Province Foundation Day, a special holiday across the province, so government offices are closed. The tourist information center's operations may also differ, so check ahead.
The paddy walls of the rice terraces are residents' precious farmland and cultural heritage. Walk only on designated paths, and don't damage the walls or step into the paddies.
When photographing residents and elders, ask permission first, and offer a small tip if requested.
Roads can be blocked by landslides during the rainy season and after typhoons. Leave a spare day in your return schedule.
Among the wooden bulul carvings and similar items, ones that look like genuinely old artifacts can raise cultural-property export issues, so buy newly made crafts instead.
Don't push yourself too hard on mountain travel and treks, and return to the village before dark.
Carry your trash back out, and don't dump waste into streams or irrigation channels. The water feeding the paddies is the village's lifeline.
During Super Typhoon Uwan in
November 2025
, landslides destroyed rice terraces and centuries-old irrigation channels in Batad and elsewhere around Banaue, and restoration work is still under way in
. Do not enter collapsed paddy walls or work zones, and follow your guide's instructions.
